extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, legal observers, and researchers following the Bill Cosby litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards, procedural rules, and evidentiary considerations that arise in criminal prosecutions and civil suits alleging sexual assault, as illustrated by the Cosby cases. Covers statute-of-limitations issues, discovery/unsealing, defamation standards, insurance coverage disputes, and other procedural doctrines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statute of limitations and legislative lookback windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether alleged offenses can be prosecuted or civilly sued depends on applicable statutes of limitations and any temporary or permanent extensions/changes to those laws (e.g., New Jersey having no statute of limitations for sexual assault in some contexts; California's temporary extensions; Nevada repealing the civil SOL for sexual assault).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prosecutors often decline to charge when the statute of limitations has expired; new statutory windows (lookback periods) or changes can reopen avenues for civil suits. The page gives examples: prosecutions declined where the alleged offense predated the removal of a statute in 1996; New Jersey and California laws that allow older claims to be brought; Nevada repealing the civil SOL enabling new suits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosecutorial charging discretion and evidentiary sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Prosecutors evaluate factors such as delay in reporting, ongoing contact between accuser and accused, possible extortion, and the overall sufficiency of evidence before bringing charges (Bruce Castor declined to bring charges in 2005 citing delay and contact; later prosecutors filed charges based on new evidence/testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay in reporting, lack of corroborating evidence, and concerns about motives can lead to decisions not to prosecute; newly uncovered evidence or unsealed testimony can prompt later charges (as when newly elected DA filed charges in 2015 based on unsealed testimony and witness interviews).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsealing confidential settlement materials and public-figure exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may justify releasing sealed documents when the defendant is a public moralist and public statements make the sealed materials relevant to public interest (judge justified releasing Constand-related documents by citing Cosby's role as a 'public moralist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release may be ordered when a public figure's statements put private conduct at issue; the page describes a judge ruling that unsealing was justified by contrast between public moralizing and alleged private conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court reporter ethics and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Court reporters' code of ethics prohibits release of testimony without contacting all parties; unauthorized release of deposition transcripts can be characterized as a 'massive breach of protocol.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The transcript of Constand's deposition was obtained from a court reporting service and released publicly; Cosby's attorneys alleged a breach of protocol by the reporting service, noting ethical rules against releasing testimony without notification and consent of parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility and evidentiary significance of deposition admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Admissions made under oath in depositions (e.g., admitting the use of sedatives or providing drugs to women) can be significant evidence and may be used by other plaintiffs once widely known or unsealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Cosby's deposition statements admitting he used sedatives to obtain cooperation and obtained Quaaludes to give to women; availability of such transcripts may allow other plaintiffs to use the testimony as evidence in their cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminal charge elements and classifications (example: aggravated indecent assault)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criminal charges are framed under statutory classifications (e.g., Cosby was charged with three counts of aggravated indecent assault based on alleged unwanted sexual contact rather than intercourse), which determine potential penalties and trial procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The charges in Montgomery County were based on alleged unwanted sexual contact from an incident in early 2004; statutory classification affects maximum penalties (the article cites potential 15–30 years and fines up to $25,000) and courtroom processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary hearing standard for proceeding to trial without victim testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Pennsylvania law a judge may find there is enough evidence to proceed to trial even if the accuser does not testify at the preliminary hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At a preliminary hearing the judge found sufficient evidence to proceed despite Constand not testifying, illustrating that preliminary-hearing standards can allow continuation to trial absent accuser testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation law standard for public figures (New York Times Co. v. Sullivan)
rubrics_metrics.description: A public figure alleging defamation must show the defendant acted with actual malice; courts also distinguish factual statements (which can be defamatory) from protected opinion under the First Amendment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cites application of NYT Co. v. Sullivan in dismissal of a defamation claim (Katherine McKee) and notes U.S. District Court decisions finding some denials to be protected opinion; plaintiffs and defendants frequently litigate whether denials are factual allegations (defamatory) or protected statements of opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insurance coverage interpretation and 'arising out of' exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Insurance-policy exclusions for sexual/physical/mental abuse can be ambiguous; ambiguous policy terms are interpreted in favor of coverage, and 'mixed' claims (allegations independent of sexual misconduct) may fall within coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIG argued the homeowner's policy did not cover the liability; Judge O'Connell found 'arising out of' ambiguous and construed ambiguity in favor of coverage, noting some complaint allegations (e.g., claims about reputation or independent factual allegations) could be read as independent of sexual misconduct and therefore covered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of mixed-claims pleading to overcome exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil complaints that include allegations independent of sexual misconduct (e.g., claims about reputational harm, actionable false statements) can be argued to fall within insurance coverage despite sexual-misconduct exclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Dickinson complaint included allegations that could be read as independent of sexual misconduct (e.g., implying Dickinson was a liar), which a judge found could place some claims within policy coverage; insurers may still appeal such holdings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marital privilege and limits on deposition questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Witnesses may invoke marital privilege to refuse to answer certain deposition questions about private spousal conversations, limiting discovery on those topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Camille Cosby relied heavily on marital privilege in deposition to refuse many questions; courts may limit questioning on privileged matters and in some situations order additional depositions on non-privileged issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural motions and defenses in civil litigation (removal, motions to dismiss, anti‑SLAPP, sanctions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendants commonly use procedural tools—motions to dismiss, removal to federal court, anti‑SLAPP motions, demurrers, and motions for sanctions—to challenge or delay suits. Courts evaluate these motions on legal standards (e.g., whether statements are protected opinion, whether jurisdiction or procedure was proper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Cosby's motions to dismiss, efforts to remove cases to federal court, anti‑SLAPP motions by Cosby and his counsel, and countersuits for defamation and legal fees; appellate courts sometimes reverse lower-court rulings on these procedural defenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of prior non-prosecution statements or agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a prior prosecutor promised not to prosecute (or otherwise made assurances) can be asserted as a defense to later prosecution; such promises may bar future charges depending on circumstances and court rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cosby's attorneys argued that Bruce Castor's 2005 decision not to prosecute amounted to a promise preventing later charges; the Pennsylvania Supreme Court later found that Cosby's agreement with a previous prosecutor prevented charging in the Constand case, resulting in overturning the conviction in 2021.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening the door for investigations despite statute limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Law enforcement may investigate allegations even when the statute of limitations has expired because older accusations may lead to more recent incidents or other victims; testimony from such investigations can still be useful in unrelated prosecutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LAPD investigated a 2008 allegation despite experts noting the SOL had expired, citing reasons such as possible links to more recent incidents and the potential to find admissible evidence for other cases; however, prosecutors later declined to charge when blocked by SOL or lack of evidence.
